_note: Channel playbooks. Item format: {t: text, c: [clause ids], b: 'doc' | 'interp'}. 'doc' means the underlying rule is stated in the NMC document. 'interp' means our recommended practice. Examples use generic wording only: no real clients or patients.

playbooks.name: Website
playbooks.intro: Design, pages, claims and modules. The website is where most of the exposure sits, because ads and SEO point to it.

allowed.t: Factual clinic details: name, address, contact, hours, departments, facilities, emergency services, accreditation status
A plain doctor directory: name, recognised qualifications, specialty, registration details, availability
Equipment and technology listed as fact
Fees and consultation charges stated plainly
Educational health information that is not promotional
Announcements: new clinic, new address, temporary closure

notAllowed.t: Testimonial pages, sliders, quote blocks, video testimonials
Review widgets, star ratings and review schema
Discount banners, countdown timers, festival offers, pop-ups

disclosure.t: Doctor name, qualifications, registration status and SMR/NMR number
Source mark on AI-generated promotional content
Awards: awarding body, year and methodology where needed to avoid misleading
Consent line and privacy link on every form

grey.t: Doctor photo on the home page or hero banner

examples.before: “Most trusted skin clinic in the city. 10,000+ happy patients.”
examples.after: “Skin clinic offering consultations in dermatology. Address, timings and contact details below.”
examples.why: Removes superlative and patient count; keeps factual details.

examples.before: Menu: Home | Services | Results | Testimonials | Contact
examples.after: Menu: Home | Services | Our doctors | Facilities | Contact
examples.why: Results and Testimonials pages are removed and redirected.

examples.before: Footer: “© 2026 Clinic. Dr. A, MD.”
examples.after: Footer: “Dr. A, MBBS, MD (Dermatology). Registered with [State] Medical Council, Reg. No. [number].”

examples.before: Hero banner: “Flat 30% off this month. Book now!”
examples.after: Hero banner: “Consultation fee: ₹[amount]. Call or book an appointment.”
examples.why: Replaces an inducement with a factual fee.

playbooks.name: Landing pages
playbooks.intro: Campaign pages are where ads land, so any problem on the page is also a problem for the ad.

allowed.t: A short factual description of the service and who provides it
Factual details: location, timings, contact, fees
Equipment named as a fact
A neutral enquiry or appointment form with a privacy notice

notAllowed.t: Offers, countdowns, limited slots, free procedures
Superlatives, comparisons, success rates, patient counts

disclosure.t: Doctor identity and registration block
AI source mark if any AI-generated promotional content is used

examples.before: “Get flawless skin in 3 sessions. Guaranteed!”
examples.after: “Skin treatments assessed and planned by a dermatologist. Results vary from person to person.”

examples.before: “Only 5 slots left. Book today for a free procedure!”
examples.after: “Book an appointment. Consultation fee: ₹[amount].”

examples.before: “4.9★ on Google. Patients love us.”
examples.after: “Clinic address, timings and facilities.”

playbooks.name: Google Ads
playbooks.intro: Ads are advertisements under §3.2. Keywords, ad copy, assets and the page the ad lands on all matter.

allowed.t: Factual ad copy: service, location, contact, timings, fees
Equipment mentioned as fact
Location, call and callout assets that are factual
Landing pages that are factual and show doctor identity
Generic and service keywords such as “dermatologist in [city]”

notAllowed.t: Superlatives and comparisons in headlines and descriptions
Image assets or sitelinks to results, testimonials or offers
Dynamic keyword insertion that can insert restricted terms

disclosure.t: Destination page must carry doctor identity and registration
AI-generated creative must be marked

grey.t: Bidding on or using “best…” as a keyword (search term, not our claim)

examples.before: Headline: “Best Hair Transplant Clinic in {city}”
examples.after: Headline: “Hair Transplant Clinic in [City]”

examples.before: Description: “10,000+ patients. 100% safe and painless. Book now!”
examples.after: Description: “Consultations with a qualified dermatologist. Call to book an appointment.”
examples.why: Removes patient count and absolute claims.

examples.before: Promotion asset: “20% off this week”
examples.after: Callout: “Consultation fee shown on website”
examples.why: Removes the inducement and points to factual fees.

examples.before: Sitelink: “Patient Results”
examples.after: Sitelink: “Our Doctors”

playbooks.name: Meta Ads
playbooks.intro: Facebook and Instagram ads are sponsored, targeted communications and count as advertising when promotional.

allowed.t: Factual awareness or educational creative with no promotion
Factual clinic announcements: opening, address change, new facility
Neutral contact or appointment campaigns with factual copy

disclosure.t: AI source mark on AI-generated promotional content
Doctor identity on the destination page

examples.before: Image: split-screen face photos labelled “Before / After”
examples.after: Image: clinic reception photo with “Appointments at [clinic], [city]”

examples.before: Primary text: “Don't ignore hair fall. You'll regret it forever!”
examples.after: Primary text: “Hair fall has many causes. A doctor can assess yours.”

examples.before: Lead form: “Win a free laser session!”
examples.after: Lead form: “Request an appointment”

playbooks.name: Social media posts
playbooks.intro: Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn and YouTube. Education is fine. Promotion, patients and offers are not.

allowed.t: Educational posts that inform and do not promote the practice
Formal announcements (opening, address, absence, fees)
Greetings on national or profession-related days
Summaries of research published in reputed journals
Factual posts about facilities and equipment

notAllowed.t: Celebrity or influencer posts and collaborations
Doctor endorsing a product or brand

disclosure.t: Doctor name, qualifications, registration status and number on the profile and in posts featuring the doctor
AI source mark on AI-generated content
Material commercial relationship in informational posts

grey.t: Hashtags and captions with calls to action

examples.before: “Our patient says: ‘Best clinic ever!’ ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐”
examples.after: “Common questions about acne treatment, answered by Dr. A, MD (Dermatology), Reg. No. [number].”
examples.why: Removes testimonial; adds education and identity.

examples.before: “Transformation Tuesday: 4 weeks, 4 sessions!”
examples.after: “How does laser hair reduction work? A short explainer.”

examples.before: “Happy Diwali! Enjoy 25% off all treatments.”
examples.after: “Wishing you a happy Diwali.”
examples.why: Keeps the greeting; removes the offer.

playbooks.name: Video shoots and reels
playbooks.intro: Scripts, shoots and edits. Many issues are decided before the camera rolls, so this playbook is mainly for the shoot plan and the edit.

allowed.t: Doctor explaining a health topic for awareness, in their own name and designation
Clinic and facility walk-throughs with no patients identifiable
Equipment shown as fact
Educational animations and explainers

notAllowed.t: Staff or celebrities recommending the clinic
Doctor endorsing a product or brand
AI voice, AI avatar or AI patient
Patients visible in frame, with names or marks

disclosure.t: Doctor name, qualifications and registration number on screen or in the caption
AI source mark on any AI-generated or materially AI-altered video

grey.t: Doctor talking to camera inside the clinic (promotional or educational?)

examples.before: Script: “I'm the No.1 hair transplant surgeon, with 5,000 successful cases.”
examples.after: Script: “Hair loss has several causes. Here is how a doctor assesses it.”

examples.before: Shot list: patient says “Thank you doctor, I look amazing!”
examples.after: Shot list: doctor explains aftercare in general terms

examples.before: Reel: before-and-after side by side with music
examples.after: Reel: 30-second explainer on how the procedure works, with risks mentioned

playbooks.name: Blog and article writing
playbooks.intro: Educational writing is the safest content we produce, if it stays educational. This playbook is about keeping it that way.

allowed.t: General health information not meant to promote the practice
Research-based articles from journal-published work by the doctor
Clear statements of risks and limits of treatments
A plain contact block

notAllowed.t: Patient case studies and “patient journey” stories
Superlatives and comparisons with other clinics
Promises of outcomes, timelines or permanence
Product or brand recommendations by the doctor

disclosure.t: Author byline with name, qualifications, registration status and SMR/NMR number
AI source mark if the article is AI-generated promotional content

grey.t: Heavy booking calls to action inside educational posts

examples.before: “Why we are the best clinic for acne scars in the city.”
examples.after: “Acne scars: types, treatment options and what to ask your doctor.”

examples.before: “Priya's story: from scars to flawless skin in 6 weeks.”
examples.after: “How long does scar treatment take? What the evidence says, and why it varies.”
examples.why: Removes a patient story and a promise.

examples.before: “Book now before it's too late for your skin!”
examples.after: “If a mole changes shape or colour, see a doctor.”

examples.before: By: Admin
examples.after: By: Dr. A, MBBS, MD (Dermatology), Reg. No. [number] ([State] Medical Council)

playbooks.name: Website and service-page content
playbooks.intro: Doctor bios, treatment pages, device pages and pricing pages. The text that sits on the site long term.

allowed.t: What the treatment is, who may need it, how it is usually done
Equipment name and purpose as a fact
Doctor bio: qualifications, registration, specialties, place of practice
Fees and packages stated plainly
Risks and limits of the treatment

disclosure.t: Doctor identity and registration block
Award year, body and methodology where an award is mentioned

grey.t: Regulatory approval claims for devices and drugs
Specialty or sub-specialty labels (for example “aesthetic physician”)

examples.before: “Dr. A is the city's top, most renowned hair transplant surgeon, with 5,000+ surgeries.”
examples.after: “Dr. A, MBBS, MS, practises hair restoration surgery. Registered with [State] Medical Council, Reg. No. [number].”
examples.why: Removes superlatives and count; adds identity.

examples.before: “Our laser is the most advanced and 100% painless.”
examples.after: “We use the [device name] laser for [purpose]. Some people feel discomfort during treatment.”

examples.before: “Permanent results in just 4 sessions.”
examples.after: “The number of sessions depends on the person and is decided by the doctor after assessment.”

playbooks.name: SEO, GBP, reviews and testimonials
playbooks.intro: Search content, Google Business Profile and online reputation. The NMC text is strongest on fake and solicited reviews, and silent on most SEO mechanics.

allowed.t: Factual titles and meta descriptions
Educational content that ranks for informational searches
A complete, factual GBP: name, address, hours, services, facilities, fees
Factual announcements on GBP: new address, temporary closure
White-hat SEO: site speed, structure, quality content

notAllowed.t: Soliciting reviews: requests, QR codes, incentives, gating
Buying or faking reviews, ratings, followers or engagement
Manipulating search rankings or visibility to mislead
Superlatives in titles, meta descriptions and headings
Review and aggregateRating schema; review widgets

disclosure.t: Doctor identity on landing pages that rank
Awards: body, date and methodology

grey.t: Existing organic reviews that appear in search

examples.before: Title: “Best Dermatologist in [City] | No.1 Skin Clinic”
examples.after: Title: “Dermatologist in [City] | [Clinic Name]”

examples.before: Front-desk script: “Please leave us a 5-star review for a free sunscreen.”
examples.after: (Stop. No review requests or incentives.)
examples.why: Soliciting and incentivising reviews is barred.

examples.before: Review reply: “Thanks Ms. R! Glad your laser session worked.”
examples.after: Review reply: “Thank you for your feedback. Please contact the clinic if you have any concerns.”
examples.why: Does not confirm patient or treatment.

examples.before: GBP post: “Monsoon offer: 40% off peels!”
examples.after: GBP update: “The clinic will be closed on [date] for maintenance.”

playbooks.name: Other channels
playbooks.intro: WhatsApp, email, influencer, print, hoardings, directories and PR. The notice names all of these as media of advertisement (§3.5).

allowed.t: Factual WhatsApp or email updates to people who opted in (address change, timings)
Health-education pamphlets for patients visiting the clinic, with no superiority claims
Hoardings with factual infrastructure and facility information
Doctor lectures on public health in own name and designation
Directory listings with accurate facts, if unpaid for ranking

notAllowed.t: WhatsApp or email offers, results, testimonials
Paid ranking of doctors on platforms
Payment to agencies or influencers linked to individual patients
Paid news or advertorials intended for promotion

disclosure.t: Material commercial relationship in informational communication
Doctor identity on electronic posts and mailers

examples.before: WhatsApp: “Diwali Dhamaka! Flat 30% off. Limited seats!”
examples.after: WhatsApp: “Our clinic timings during Diwali are [dates and times].”

examples.before: Hoarding: “No.1 Skin Clinic. 25 years of trust.”
examples.after: Hoarding: “[Clinic name]. Dermatology. [Address]. [Phone]”

examples.before: Influencer reel: “I got my skin done here and I love it!”
examples.after: (Stop. No influencer promotion.)
